doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Copying records, practicing and listening
summary: He copied the records daily, learned theory from rock & roll, and advises equal listening and practice time.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Can you define what you were — how were you practicing? Were you copying?
You were trying to get what these trumpet players were playing?

Yes and I thought that I was like the worst trumpet player that ever lived, because I couldn’t play a lot of the stuff that was on the records. Try to play along with Maynard Ferguson and I’m going, “They don’t even have the fingerings in the book for this, so how am I supposed to do this?” You know. So I said, “Well I’ll just use the ones an octave lower.” And then it worked and you know so, and I played in band, in middle school band and when I finally — I remember when I was in middle school band that we were reading like a simple march book, the Bennett Band Book I remember it was a little, you know one of these things. And they had like easy versions of marches. And they

started playing and I said what? How come there’s three eighth notes in a beat? I don’t get this. Because it was 6/8 you see. And I didn’t understand how 6/8 worked and — I could play it, because once I heard somebody play it I figured it out you know. But I really was, I mean I always practiced. When I was in junior high school I practiced at least a couple of hours a day. At least. And I listened. See? And I always tell people today, no matter what lessons they’re taking, I say, “Practicing is a good thing.” I said, “If you only like to practice a half hour a day and you just want to learn to play a little bit and play in a group then you only have to listen a half hour a day.” I said, “If you want to practice more than that then you have to practice the equivalent time listening. Otherwise you have no vocabulary. All you have is words. You have just words and they don’t make any sense to anybody.” See you know and the inflection, I said, “You have to learn the vernacular language of whatever is on the recording.” If I’m listening to a classical symphony — which I did — I worked at Lockheed where my dad worked, Lockheed Aircraft at Kennedy Airport when it was there, before they moved. And I was the receiving clerk one summer. And I had one of those — you know those radios that have the antenna was the handle?

Well that’s what I had. And it was green and it had that patent leather all over it. And I used to listen to WPAT, New Jersey, which was right over the river from the airport. And it was all classical. Because by that time I was going to go to Eastman. I was in Eastman at the time. And these guys, they had to come and they had runners for parts you know. And they would come and say, “I want this part here, number 4 —” I said, “Wait,” I said, “what is that music you’re listening to? I said, “That’s the music you’re going to have to listen to before I get your part.” You know cement heads I was working with. But I understood. I understood all that. But I listened all the time. Because when I found music, and I tell students the same thing. I said — I listen to rock & roll. And the reason I did was because well I was a kid and we all listened to rock & roll. And I said, you know these chords that they’re playing, some notes stay the same and some notes change. And most of the time they don’t change much. So I was learning theory right away. See? And I learned to play with those ideas in my mind. So well that note stays the same almost the whole time. I can work off of that note you know what I mean? I was clueless, you know?
